user: Explain in brief what do you mean by Calico or Kubernetes network policies?
assistant: Calico and Kubernetes network policies are used to control network traffic in a Kubernetes cluster.
Kubernetes network policies are a native Kubernetes feature that allows you to specify the network traffic that you want to allow or block to and from a pod within a cluster. They control traffic based on protocol, port, and source or destination IP addresses, and can also filter traffic based on pod and namespace labels.
Calico network policies, on the other hand, are a set of Kubernetes network policies provided by the Calico project. They offer additional features such as allowing or blocking network traffic on specific network interfaces regardless of the pod's source or destination IP address or CIDR, and blocking inbound traffic to Kubernetes LoadBalancer or NodePort services. Calico policies can be applied using the calicoctl command line.
user: Is my app accessible on all public and private cluster network interfaces?
assistant: Yes. The default network policies for a cluster allow all public outbound network traffic and enable public inbound traffic to specific cluster components, such as Kubernetes NodePort, LoadBalancer, and Ingress services. All private traffic is allowed by default by the allow-all-private-default policy. Therefore, if no additional policies have been set up, your app should be accessible on all public and private cluster network interfaces. However, any other inbound network traffic from the internet to your worker nodes that aren't specified in the default policies gets blocked.
This is the default behavior, and your specific cluster configuration may vary. It is always a good idea to review your current network policies to ensure they meet your security requirements.
user: Which ports are accessible from the public internet?
assistant: Only the public node port and public NLB port are exposed to the public internet.
user: How can I make my containerized app accessible over the internet?
assistant: To make your containerized app accessible over the internet, you can create both a public Network Load Balancer (NLB) and a private NLB in a classic cluster. Portable public and private IP addresses are static floating IPs and don't change when a worker node is removed. If the worker node that the NLB IP address is on is removed, a Keepalive daemon that constantly monitors the IP automatically moves the IP to another worker node. You can assign any port to your NLB, and the NLB serves as the external entry point for incoming requests for the app. To access the NLB from the internet, you can use the public IP address of your NLB and the assigned port in the format <IP\_address>:<port>. You can also create DNS entries for NLBs by registering the NLB IP addresses with subdomains. When you expose an app with an NLB service, your app is automatically made available over the service's NodePorts too.
